claims.text: The dynamic strength–ductility response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by a temperature- and strain-rate-dependent transition between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Lower temperatures promote deformation twinning in FeNiCrMn.
Higher strain rates promote deformation twinning in FeNiCrMn.
Enhanced twin formation provides additional strain hardening.
Enhanced twin formation increases yield strength.
Higher temperatures and lower strain rates cause dislocation slip to dominate deformation in FeNiCrMn.
Slip-dominated deformation favors greater ductility.
As-cast and homogenized FeNiCrMn with minimized casting defects has a predominantly single-phase microstructure similar to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi is a single-phase FCC alloy.
The strength–ductility balance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi arises from an interplay of deformation mechanisms similar to that proposed for FeNiCrMn.
At low temperature and high strain rate, the activation energy for twinning is lower relative to that for slip.
Twinning can boost strength without severely compromising ductility in FeNiCrMn.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate specimens will have higher twin densities than high-temperature, low-strain-rate specimens.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate specimens will have higher dynamic yield strengths than high-temperature, low-strain-rate specimens.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate specimens will have greater strain-hardening rates than high-temperature, low-strain-rate specimens.
The proposed mechanism preserves a favorable strength–ductility balance across the tested regimes.
The hypothesis is applicable to low-defect, as-cast and homogenized FeNiCrMn between 77 K and 600 K and strain rates of approximately 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1.
Significant microstructural heterogeneity or testing outside the specified temperature and strain-rate ranges may change the response.
A controlled temperature-by-strain-rate test matrix with TEM and EBSD can compare twin fraction, dislocation structures, yield strength, and work-hardening rate.

Failure to observe a systematic twin-fraction increase at low temperature and high strain rate, or failure of strength and hardening to correlate with the proposed mechanism shift, would falsify the hypothesis.
